inline.s: Joyfully Returning to Mount Kuang: Six Poems

Late in life I slipped the bonds that tangled me;
hollowing out the mind, one enters Chan with ease.
I have stolen life until this day,
at peace and glad in my remaining years.
Old debts of courtesy are all discharged;
good karmic bonds, I trust, have not failed me.
My spirit hides in a handful of earth —
right there a blue lotus will well up.

Illness: Two Poems

Long have I wearied of the body’s burden;
how should I bear age and sickness invading?
I am ashamed my samādhi is shallow,
and feel the source of illness deepen.
Understanding the Dharma, one is free of all marks;
contemplating emptiness, one sees this mind.
Would you transcend the road of birth and death?
Do not seek it outside.
After the Porridge, Walking Meditation: An Instruction

Porridge done, I walk slowly in meditation,
following the stream, not asking the distance.
My feet are like broken silk thread;
my body is light as a wisp of cloud.
Stepping on, the mountain light shines through;
coming back, the moonlight is bright.
No need to enter the room again —
just listen to the night bell.

Roaming the Star Crags with Ding Youwu and Wang Weiwu; Not Yet Returned, I Write My Thoughts

For viewing wonders and seeking the strange, I yield to Suqiu;
and here I meet a Xiao Shi to roam with me.
A thousand hills cling close like a twin dragon’s wings;
ten thousand gorges race toward one leaf of a boat.
Who can find the cinnabar in the cave?
When will the herbs in the clouds be gathered?
Do not watch the chess-players beneath the pine —
half a game is enough to turn one’s hair white.

I Once Roamed the Wangu Temple in Hedong with Master Miaofeng; Hearing It Is Now Restored, I Write This to Send My Thoughts

Forty years ago I passed this way begging food,
where the Jetavana monastery stands beside the Ganges.
The Zhongtiao Mountains rise like a blue lotus crown;
the clouds of Mount Hua surge like waves on a jade sea.
A thousand households in its walls are Shravasti again;
the Dharma-body three times unfolds and turns this Saha world.
When shall I once more shoulder the dragon-taming staff,
and again hold the karma rite before Mangu’s couch?
Climbing the Water Tower at Wujing

Threading clouds, crossing the gorge, over level fields,
I walk the stream to its source and see the market town.
A single thread of river reaches the great sea;
all around, mountain hues embrace a blue lotus.
The tower stands where water and moon make a cool land;
a man enters an empty dwelling, a heaven of freedom.
It might be Peach Blossom Spring, that refuge from Qin —
only the boats that come and go are not fishing boats.

A Birthday Greeting for Layman Miao Juexiu

All my life my tracks have gone east and west;
come old age, how could I choose a tree to perch on?
Though the spine be hard as iron,
what is to be done when the shin bones are soft as mud?
At leisure I watch clouds rise from the sheer gorge;
sitting, I lean on a thousand peaks and hear the birds cry.
No need to pick out phrases beyond words:
the sights and sounds before me are the whole presentation.

Against the cliff I built myself a hut of thatch;
just enough to hold this body, a single niche.
If only the mind’s source returns to clear stillness,
let the world’s affairs go to foolish simplicity.
When the sun is three poles high, I still lie long abed;
clouds seal the ten-foot room and let no caller in.
Let Buddha and Patriarch have their traces cut off —
why must they be ranged three before and three behind?

In the hidden cliff the orchids keep a lingering fragrance;
the gentle pine wind carries a secret scent.
Borrowing the perfume of hearing to open the ground of mind
is better than pouring sweet dew into a withered belly.
Mind after mind goes straight into the lotus treasury;
thought after thought ever lights the radiance of prajñā.
Contentment itself mounts to the Tuṣita realm —
why toil to seek the West beyond this?

Why did I love to leave home in those years?
I cannot forget the old worn cassock I put on.
Only because debts from many lives were not yet settled —
it was not that a single thought went wrong before.
Half a lifetime of karmic ties, all a dream;
a hundred years of delusive thought, no more than empty flowers.
Coming back, only the green hills remain —
how could I bear to trade gold for sand?
Sick in Bed
Replying to Commissioner Lu Jingye

Your tall carriage has crossed these empty hills how many times,
passing every peak and breaking straight through the pass.
I have a tongue, yet cannot answer the secret truth;
forgetting all contrivance, one may well face a withered face.
Flying snow comes and shines cold upon us;
gazing into blue clouds, the thought grows idler still.
From afar I recall where you sit upright at the camp gate —
Mount Kuang is ever between your brows.
Sent to the Chan Monk Jingguang of Mount Yang

Since you returned from asking the Dharma at Mount Kuang,
the years have passed and letters have grown few.
As for me, I have entered the patience of the un-born;
I know you always inquire into the upward matter.
After rain the clouds part and the mountain’s bones are lean;
in late spring, with warm sun, the fern shoots are fat.
When shall we shake the staff before the couch again,
and hold up the fine-spun robe that came from the West?
Remembering Mountain Dwelling: Six Poems (with a Preface)
While in prison it was as though I dwelt deep in the mountains; hence these verses.

White snow lies before the eaves;
it flies here day after day, the same as ever.
If you had no mind,
how could you keep dwelling here with me?

Flowing water is not sound;
the bright moon was never form.
Sound and form have no relation —
who can understand this state?

Where does the wind come from?
A crowd of sounds stirs the rocky cave.
Listen in stillness: there is no sound at all —
how then can there be rising and ceasing?

This body is among a thousand crags;
the road before the gate goes nowhere.
In the still silence, who is my companion?
Only a few pines.
Mooring on the Pearl River
Songs of the Dharma Ground in the Army: Four Poems

At dawn I hear the battle drums;
at dusk I hear the golden chime.
Though motion and stillness differ,
only the one who knows the tune can appreciate it.

Banners blot out the floating clouds;
streamers shadow the morning sun.
Just look at the mechanism of killing and sparing —
soldiers are not like the secrecy of Chan.
The Dharma drum shakes the dragon palace;
the shouting moves heaven and earth.
How like the wind through many hollows,
sighing forth the breath of the Great Clod!

I once sat on the Eastern Sea,
where raging waves broke the mountains in fury.
Now I hear thunder that shakes the sky;
entering my ears, the mind is only more at ease.
